extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of comedy/playwriting; readers of literary theory on humour
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic principles and practical archetypes for creating and understanding comedic effects on stage and in literature, drawn from philosophical and theatrical examples. Focuses on mechanisms (repetition, inversion, mechanical imagery) that produce laughter and how to deploy them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person-as-thing (mechanization of person)
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sancho Panza tumbled like a football, Baron Munchausen as a cannon-ball, clowns whose movements suggest rubber balls or wooden dummies. The comic arises when human beings are perceived as objects through attitudes, movements, or gradual suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion (vague-to-clear transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear and distinct is the method of suggestion par excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological analogue: hypnotist who slowly makes perceptions indefinite and then clarifies them; falling asleep sees shapeless masses solidify into objects. Poetic devices (rhythm, rhyme, assonance) can lull the imagination into accepting the suggested image (e.g., Regnard and Figaro lines). Use slow, graduated hints to make an absurd image acceptable and thus comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life + mechanical arrangement (central definition of comic situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY ARRANGEMENT OF ACTS AND EVENTS IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US, IN A SINGLE COMBINATION, THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general law: comedy arises where the appearance of living, spontaneous action coexists with the perception of automatism or mechanism. When actions look like they are governed by springs, strings, or rigid gears rather than free life, we laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box mechanism (repetition & rebound)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic type in which a force (feeling or action) is repeatedly repressed and springs back like a jack-in-the-box; the comic tempo is the rebound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage examples: Punch and Judy, the policeman repeatedly felled and springing up; Sganarelle vs Pancrace where characters 'rebound' on and off stage; Monsieur Purgon and Argan's recurring exclamation marking TEMPO. This archetype often manifests as repetition that signals an underlying mechanical struggle between two forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-repetition as symbolism of mechanical tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition of a word is not comic in itself but because it symbolizes a mechanical play of moral elements: a repressed feeling that repeatedly bursts forth and an idea that delights in repressing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dorine's repeated 'Et tartuffe?' as a spring released and then pushed back; Scapin exploiting Geronte's avarice; Harpagon's recurring 'No dowry wanted!' The author should make repetition reflect an internal automatism (something mechanical within something living).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack / manipulated character
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy where a character seems free but is actually a toy in the hands of another (a dancing-jack whose strings are pulled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scapin manipulating Geronte and Argante; scenes where one character vacillates between two contrary opinions and is personified by opposing forces. The playwright often personifies the opposing decisions so that the spectator can perceive the strings being pulled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball / cumulative progression
rubrics_metrics.description: An effect which grows by arithmetical progression: a small cause accumulates into a large and often unexpected result (rolling snow-ball, toy-soldier topple, house of cards collapse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: picture-stories where one mishap triggers another; Chicanneau's lawsuits within lawsuits; modern comedies where a lost object (e.g., a hat) propels ever-widening mishaps. The mechanism is often reversible/circular, and returning to the starting-point (futile, circular effort) is itself comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence/absentmindedness as source of comic mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid mechanism detected in human affairs is perceived as a kind of ABSENTMINDEDNESS on the part of life; laughter functions as a social corrective to this inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: When events or people act as if 'unmindful' of continuity or individuality (coincidences, conjunctures), the mechanical appearance provokes laughter because it points out an imperfection that society corrects by ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between life and mechanism yields three methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Life’s outward characteristics (continuous evolution, irreversibility, perfect individuality) have counterparts that produce comic effects: REPETITION, INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE OF SERIES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three processes form the abstract archetypes for comic methods. The text proceeds to examine them (repetition is developed in this chunk); writers should consider which counterpart to life they are invoking when crafting comic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational repetition (reproduced scenes across tempo/groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of an entire situation (not merely a word) across acts or among different groups of characters produces comedy when the scene is complex yet naturally reintroduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ecole des femmes reproducing a single incident in three tempi; George Dandin's three-tempo structure; masters/servants repeating analogous scenes (Amphitryon, Depit amoureux). Repetition is funnier when the scene is richly constructed and the recurrence feels plausibly integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of opposing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character vacillates between two contrary impulses, a comic author personifies these two opposing decisions (gives them visible actors or distinct voices) so the 'strings' can be perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Panurge asking Tom, Dick, and Harry about marriage—author personifies the two poles of decision so the spectator can see the mechanical play. This makes the internal oscillation externally comic.
